meta.title: Radiation Cancellation
meta.subtitle: A multipole model of the leak from $\pi$ shift Bragg grating cavities
meta.author: Evyatar Rubin

items.text: \textbf{The leak splits into electric and magnetic harmonics.}
items.detail: A small geometry change shifts each harmonic linearly, so several knobs are set by one linear solve.

items.text: \textbf{The plain TE leak is mostly beyond the dipole.}
items.detail: Dipoles carry 14\,\% of it; 95\,\% lies in the first five orders.

items.text: \textbf{Plain TE: ten cancelled harmonics could raise $Q$ at -3 dB from 12\,900 to about 10$^5$.}

items.detail: Radiation is only part of its loss; removing all of it gives ×1.4 to ×1.9.

frames.heading: Part I: The model
frames.subheading: How a geometry change alters the radiated leak.

frames.title: Johnson et al.\ cancelled one dominant harmonic with one knob

items: One harmonic carries almost all the loss.
The loss is spread over several harmonics.
The model predicts what each knob can remove.

frames.note: Johnson's 2D example has one field component, $E_z$, so each order has one coefficient. Our 3D field has two polarizations, so each $(l,m)$ has two.

frames.title: The leak is a sum of electric and magnetic harmonics
frames.notes: A: far-field amplitude in direction r-hat; Delta-epsilon = epsilon - n_ox^2; E: cavity field at resonance; k: wavenumber in oxide. X_lm: vector spherical harmonic (Jackson ch. 9). alpha_lm: magnetic coefficient, beta_lm: electric coefficient. Equivalently alpha_lm = 4 pi (-i)^l Int Delta-epsilon j_l(kr) X*_lm . E d^3r, the source form used to see how a local change moves a harmonic.

blocks.label: Far field.
blocks.text: Everything that differs from the oxide radiates:

blocks.label: Harmonics.
blocks.text: The same coefficients from the far field, or from the source:
$\mathbf{X}_{lm}$: vector spherical harmonic, the angular pattern of order ($l$, $m$); $j_l$: spherical Bessel function. $\alpha$ magnetic, $\beta$ electric.

frames.title: A feature adds its own coefficients to those of the leak
frames.notes: c: list of all alpha_lm and beta_lm of the cavity leak, normalized per unit stored energy, so ||c||^2 is proportional to 1/Q_rad (a feature that only lowers the coupling then cannot look like cancellation). b: change of all coefficients per unit knob strength q; it contains the feature's own radiation, the change of the cavity field and the resonance shift, so it is measured (two runs, +h and -h). Validity: the feature holds a small part of the mode energy.

blocks.label: Leak:
blocks.text: its coefficients $\mathbf{c}$ = ($\alpha_{lm}$, $\beta_{lm}$), per unit stored energy.

blocks.label: Feature:
blocks.text: strength $q$ (for example a tooth width); adds $\mathbf{b}$ per unit $q$, measured.
Linear while the feature is small: runs at $\pm h$ give equal and opposite changes.

frames.title: One knob: the best strength follows from $dP/dq$ = 0

blocks.equation: \text{2. Lowest loss where the slope is zero: }\frac{dP}{dq}=0\;\Rightarrow\;q_{*}=-\frac{\mathrm{Re}\langle b,c\rangle}{\left|b\right|^2}

blocks.text: $\eta^2$: the fraction of the leak this knob can remove. Set too strong, at $2q_*$ the loss is back at its original value.

frames.notes: eta^2 is computed from a knob's measured response b and the measured leak c. No knob has been measured yet; the Part II tables assume ideal knobs, whose eta^2 equals the share of the harmonics they cancel.

frames.title: Several knobs: one linear problem
frames.note: $K$ target harmonics; $B_S$, $\mathbf{w}$, $\mathbf{v}$: their response, two runs per knob. Exact with $2K+2$ knobs, least squares with fewer.

frames.caption: Share of the radiated power per harmonic; +$m$ and -$m$ are equal (mirror symmetry in $y$), so each cell is their sum. $N$ = 98, $T$ = 0.912, mode 19.1\,$\mu$m.

frames.title: Overshoot apodization: the leak is spread over many orders
frames.caption: $N$ = 98, $T$ = 0.973, mode 19.6\,$\mu$m. Dipoles hold 6\,\%; half of the power is above $l$ = 12.

frames.title: Plain TM at the same mode width
frames.caption: Corrugation 325\,nm, $N$ = 98, $T$ = 0.915, mode 19.2\,$\mu$m. Dipoles hold 11\,\%; 74\,\% is in $l \le 5$, with a tail along the waveguide axis.

frames.title: Plain TE: cancelling ten harmonics could raise $Q$ up to ×9
frames.note: Estimated for ideal knobs ($\eta^2$ equal to the cancelled share $f$): $Q$ at -3 dB = 12\,900/(1 - $f$). Example, 5 largest: 12\,900/0.31 = 41\,000.

frames.title: Overshoot: cancellation reaches only part of its loss
frames.note: Estimated for ideal knobs. Radiation ($Q_\mathrm{rad}$ = 2.2 × 10$^6$) is a third of the internal loss, so 1/$Q_i$ = (1 - $f$)/$Q_\mathrm{rad}$ + 1/$Q_\mathrm{other}$.

frames.title: Conclusions
items: \textbf{Model:} harmonics, the linear effect of a feature, one linear solve for all knobs.
\textbf{Plain TE:} a compact leak; about ten harmonics would have to cancel for a large gain.
\textbf{Overshoot:} a spread leak, and radiation is only part of its loss: tens of percent.
\textbf{Open question:} does radiation dominate the overshoot's loss? That sets how far cancellation can go.

frames.title: Next steps
items: \textbf{Decide:} measure the overshoot's own loss budget and $Q$ at -3 dB at a fixed simulation time; continue only if radiation dominates.
\textbf{Choose the perturbation:} the geometry change near the junction that reaches the largest harmonics, with its response measured.
\textbf{Optimize:} solve for the knob settings at fixed width and resonance, then validate with one run.
